transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-07 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~78 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Elliot (Redwood SE), Marissa (Redwood SE), Priya (Horizon CTO), Tomas, Michael, Sara

Summary / context (auto): HorizonAI running mixed Llama/Mistral/Qwen in prod at low latency targets. Looking to tune RoPE settings and reduce MoE routing token cost while keeping tail latency below 200ms for 95th. On-prem VPC option with strict egress rules considered.

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros, then elliot will jump into the NUMA / memory affinity items.
[00:22] Priya: Hi, thanks. our main ask: 95th <200ms for short chat queries, and we want to cut token costs on MoE spikes. also compliance needs keep data inside our VPC.
[00:35] Elliot: cool. i pulled together two symptom sets — one is tail-latency spikes when we hit long contexts with Qwen-14B, the other is uneven GPU utilization when routing to experts in the moe model.
[01:05] Tomas: yes, the Qwen traces show big variance; sometimes tokens cluster to a particular attention pattern and GPU memory thrashes.
[01:22] Marissa: first thing i want to confirm: are you doing NUMA pinning on your CPU side for KV cache allocation? a lot of on-prem setups see massive slowdowns when the code touches the 'wrong' NUMA region during KV cache prefetch.
[01:40] Michael: we haven't been explicitly pinning; we rely on default kernel setups. that's probably it — our infra team tried pinning once but saw mixed results.
[01:55] Elliot: okay, two immediate wins: 1) allocate KV cache on the same NUMA node as the GPU's PCIe root complex; 2) use hugepages for large KV tables to reduce TLB pressure. We've got scripts that do the numa bind and check page faults.
[02:24] Priya: script would be great. is that safe for multi-tenant hosts?
[02:32] Jordan: good question — for Dedicated or Private you'll control tenancy anyway; for hosted multi-tenant it's riskier. but since Horizon is moving to a VPC-on-prem host we can recommend exclusive NUMA bindings.
[02:50] Tomas: another observation: our RoPE scaling seems to cause token affinity to drift — long contexts just get lower logits later in the sequence. any suggestions?
[03:08] Elliot: RoPE (rotary pos enc) interaction with quantized kernels is subtle. when you reduce precision, phase wrapping errors accumulate. we've seen a mitigation by rescaling RoPE base (the theta) slightly and applying per-layer interpolation for late layers. it's a surgical change — we call it 'RoPE surgery' internally.
[03:36] Marissa: also consider 'positional decay' — lowering effective RoPE magnitude for tokens beyond 2k can reduce softmax saturation and reduce unnecessary expert routing in MoE.
[03:53] Priya: wait, does that impact quality for instructions? we care about coherence over long dialogues.
[04:05] Elliot: tradeoff, yes. you can gradually decay RoPE past a cutoff and compensate with a KV cache that preserves exact keys. the combo keeps immediate context quality but avoids overemphasizing far tokens in routing.
[04:28] Tomas: interesting — we do use a long KV cache, but it's sparsely warmed. can Redwood's runtime prefetch KV entries?
[04:40] Marissa: yes — we have a KV prefetch / prewarm mechanism. the approach is workload-aware prefetching: look at request histogram, prewarm top-k prefixes into local GPU-resident cache during load spikes. the challenge is safe eviction and bandwidth.
[05:05] Michael: bandwidth is our worry — we have a 25Gb link between host and GPU chassis for the on-prem box. prefetching too aggressively will starve other flows.
[05:16] Elliot: that's where adaptive prefetching helps — set a network budget and a prefetch budget per model. also use delta-encoding for KV blobs — we've replaced naive full-key copies with compressed deltas for Mistral and Qwen and seen 3x reduction.
[05:40] Priya: compression might add CPU overhead though?
[05:46] Marissa: yes but doing compression in a separate core with affinity and using DMA can hide most of it. plus with hugepages and pinned memory, CPU cycles for compression are small relative to the benefit.
[05:58] [crosstalk briefly as someone grabs a doc]
[06:15] Jordan: let's pivot to MoE costs — Tomas shared that spikes in routing increase token unit cost ~2.7x during certain prompts. can you unpack what triggers spikes?
[06:30] Tomas: spikes happen when queries pivot to niche topics; the router picks small expert sets that are memory-hot. also when we don't cache expert outputs, repeated tokens retrigger routing.
[06:45] Elliot: two mitigation levers: 1) routing smoothing — add a soft penalty to switching experts per-token to keep continuity, 2) expert affinity caching — cache recent expert outputs keyed by prefix hash to avoid re-routing identical patterns.
[07:05] Marissa: bonus: use a reduced-precision routing pass — run the router in int8 to pick experts then run the selected experts in higher precision. routing is cheap but sensitive to noise, so calibrate thresholds.
[07:22] Priya: does int8 router hurt accuracy?
[07:26] Elliot: small effect; we calibrate with a holdout set. it's about keeping stability, not absolute per-token score. most customers accept minor deltas for big cost wins.
[07:40] Michael: what about scheduling? Our k8s cluster schedules pods across sockets and that seems to cause cross-socket DMA.
[07:52] Marissa: for on-prem we recommended node-pinning policies and a kube-scheduler plugin that respects PCIe locality. also ensure the device-plugin reports NUMA topology.
[08:10] Tomas: batching: we currently use static microbatch of 4. Redwood recommends adaptive batching with a 20ms latency cap, right?
[08:22] Elliot: yes, our adaptive batcher increases batch up to a cap where predicted 95p stays below your SLO. It also does token-aware batching — grouping requests by expected output length reduces jitter.
[08:40] Priya: any gotchas for embeddings-heavy traffic?
[08:45] Marissa: embeddings are cheaper but high concurrency; use a separate pool with lower-prewarm to avoid stealing KV memory. Also quantize embeddings table to fp16 or int8 depending on quality needs.
[08:58] [15:00 minute mark omitted but timestamps continue every ~30-90s]
[09:20] Tomas: quant profiles — we ran Qwen through a generic int8 profile and saw spikes in hallucination for code-gen. suggestions?
[09:33] Elliot: create a model-specific calibration with per-layer clip points. For Qwen, keep first 3 transformer layers at fp16 and quantize later layers. For Mistral, per-head sym quant works better. We'll send profiles.
[09:52] Jordan: we'll share recommended quant config in the repo. hoping that avoids repeated trial-and-error.
[10:05] Priya: about security: can Redwood's private deployment use our KMS? we need to ensure keys never leave our HSM.
[10:16] Jordan: yes, private/control plane supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integration — you control master keys, Redwood only sees wrapped keys. we'll add the certs/arch doc to the doc bundle.
[10:28] Michael: network ports? our security team only allows a short list.
[10:33] Marissa: standard: 443 outbound for control, and a small set of ephemeral ports for prewarm syncs, can be configured for peering only. we'll share a VPC peering checklist.
[10:50] Tomas: SLOs — if we prewarm KV aggressively, what is cost delta?
[10:58] Elliot: typical numbers: prewarm for top-5 prefixes reduces per-token cost by ~18-25% for hotspot workloads but increases memory pressure. For MoE, expert caching can shave 30% off routing-induced peak cost.
[11:15] Priya: can we see those figures with our traces?
[11:20] Elliot: yes, action item — send traces; we'll run the scripts and return histograms plus an estimated token cost curve.
[11:36] Marissa: also watch RoPE sway: we recommend two experiments — 1) soft RoPE decay after token 2048 with KV backed rescue; 2) per-layer theta tweak for quantized runtimes. we'll include small patches for both.
[11:56] Priya: ok, if we do that, how do we measure regression?
[12:02] Jordan: use a small eval harness with instruction/regression pairs; Redwood has a suggested prompt set. we'll share the harness and metrics (perplexity, exact-match on checkpoints).
[12:17] Michael: scheduling the on-prem minibench — we prefer a 2-GPU test using your runtime. can Redwood bring a prebuilt container?
[12:28] Jordan: yes — we'll provide a signed image and a manifest. you can run it inside your VPC with local KMS.
[12:40] Tomas: final: any quick wins we can apply in the next week?
[12:46] Elliot: enable NUMA pinning for KV, turn on adaptive batching with a tight 20ms budget, and enable int8 router with a conservative threshold. those three should cut tail and cost quickly.
[13:00] Priya: great. thanks.

Recap (auto): Agreed next steps and owners. Redwood to share scripts, quant profiles, and prewarm code. Horizon to provide traces and network details. Plan an on-prem 2-GPU run in two weeks.

End of transcript.
